text: Abstract

This report presents the design and implementation of a Distribution Management System (DMS), a console-based application written in the C programming language. The system models a real-life product distribution chain consisting of three levels: a company, its dealers, and the retailers connected to those dealers. The company holds products in a central warehouse, dealers purchase stock from the company, and retailers purchase stock from their assigned dealer. The project was intentionally built using only fundamental programming concepts, namely variables, arrays, loops, conditional statements and functions, so that every part of the code remains easy to read and explain. The complete program is divided into six source modules that communicate through header files, demonstrating how a beginner-friendly project can still follow a clean, modular structure.
Keywords: C programming, distribution chain, modular design, arrays, stock management, console application
1. Introduction
1.1 Background

In the real world, most products do not travel directly from a manufacturer to a customer. Instead they pass through a distribution chain. A company produces goods and stores them in a warehouse. Dealers (also called distributors) buy these goods in bulk and store them regionally. Retailers, which are the local shops that customers actually visit, buy smaller quantities from a nearby dealer. Keeping track of how much stock exists at every level of this chain is a classic inventory management problem.

This project simulates that exact flow in software. Although commercial distribution systems are large database-driven applications, the same core logic, checking stock, transferring quantities and recording the result, can be expressed with simple arrays and functions in C. Building it this way makes the underlying idea very clear, because nothing is hidden behind frameworks or libraries.
1.2 Motivation

The main motivation behind this project was to practise writing a multi-file C program that solves a realistic problem while staying inside the topics covered in a first programming course. Most beginner exercises fit in a single file, but real software is always split into modules. This project was a chance to learn how separate .c files share data and functions through header files, and how a program can be organised so that each file has one clear responsibility.
1.3 Objectives
To build a working simulation of a three-level distribution chain (company, dealer, retailer).
To allow each type of user to view the stock that belongs to them.
To let dealers order products from the company, and retailers order from their dealer, with automatic stock transfer.
To reject invalid operations such as ordering more than the available stock or entering an unknown product ID.
To keep the entire codebase limited to basic C concepts: if-else, loops, arrays and functions.
To organise the program into separate modules that communicate through header files.
1.4 Scope of the Project

The system is a console application that runs in a terminal. All data lives in memory while the program runs; when the program exits, the state resets to the default sample data. Features such as file storage, passwords, prices and payments were deliberately left out to keep the focus on the distribution logic itself. These are discussed later as future improvements.
2. System Overview
2.1 The Distribution Chain

The whole system is built around one idea: stock flows downward through the chain, and orders flow upward. A retailer asks its dealer for products, and the dealer asks the company. Every successful order subtracts a quantity from the seller's stock and adds the same quantity to the buyer's stock, so the total amount of product in the system never changes on its own.

text: 3. System Design
3.1 Modular Architecture

The program is split into six modules. Each module is a pair of files: a header file (.h) that declares what the module offers, and a source file (.c) that contains the actual code. Any module that wants to use another module simply includes its header. This is the standard way C programs are organised, and it means each file can be read and understood on its own.

rows: Program entry point; shows the main menu and routes to the right panel
Declares and stores all shared arrays; loads the default sample data
All printing helpers: menus, tables, error and success messages

Dealer panel: login, view stock, order from the company
Retailer panel: login, view stock, order from the dealer
caption: The six modules and what each one is responsible for
Module relationships: the three panels all read and write the shared data module and print through the display module

text: 3.2 How the Modules Communicate

All shared information lives in data.c as global arrays. The header file data.h re-declares each array with the extern keyword, which tells the compiler that the variable exists in another file. When dealer.c includes data.h, it gains access to the exact same arrays that company.c and retailer.c use. This is why an order placed in the dealer panel is immediately visible in the company panel: there is only one copy of the data, shared by everyone.
Key idea: a variable is DEFINED once in one .c file, but can be DECLARED with extern in a header so that every other file can use it.
3.3 Data Structures

Instead of structures or dynamic memory, the project uses parallel arrays: several arrays that share the same index. For example, index 0 of product_id, product_name and company_stock together describe the first product (ID 1, "Rice", 100 units). Stock owned by dealers and retailers is stored in two-dimensional arrays, where the row selects the dealer or retailer and the column selects the product.

text: 4.2 The Main Menu (main.c)

Execution starts in main(). It first calls init_data() to load the sample data, then enters a do-while loop that keeps showing the main menu until the user types 0. A chain of if-else statements sends the user to the correct panel.
4.3 Searching by ID (the found flag pattern)

Users refer to products, dealers and retailers by their ID numbers, but arrays are accessed by index. The program converts an ID to an index with a simple linear search. A flag variable named found starts at 0 and becomes 1 if the loop finds a match; if the loop finishes with found still 0, the ID does not exist and an error is shown. This little pattern appears everywhere in the project.
4.4 Placing an Order

Ordering is the heart of the system. Before any stock moves, the program runs three checks in order: the product must exist, the quantity must be positive, and the seller must actually have that many units. Only when all three checks pass does the transfer happen, and it is just two lines of arithmetic: subtract from the seller, add to the buyer.

caption: Order processing: three validation gates protect the stock transfer

text: 4.5 The Display Module

All printing goes through helper functions in display.c, such as print_menu_header(), print_table_product_row() and print_order_summary(). Centralising the printing has two benefits: every screen in the program looks consistent, and the panel files stay short because they never repeat formatting code. The tables are drawn with plain text characters using printf width specifiers such as %-20s, which pads a string to 20 characters so the columns line up.
5. Compilation and Running

Because the program is spread across six .c files, all of them must be compiled and linked together. The GCC compiler does this in one command. Each .c file is compiled separately into machine code, and the linker then joins them into a single executable named dms. If any module called a function that no other module defines, the linker would report an undefined reference error, which is how C enforces that the modules fit together.

cd DMS
gcc -o dms main.c data.c company.c dealer.c retailer.c display.c
./dms

7. Limitations and Future Work
7.1 Current Limitations
Data is not saved to disk, so all changes are lost when the program closes.
There are no prices or payments; orders only move quantities.
Products, dealers and retailers cannot be added while the program is running; they are fixed in init_data().
There is no password protection; anyone can log in as any dealer or retailer by choosing an ID.
Non-numeric input to scanf can confuse the menus, since input is read as plain integers.
7.2 Future Improvements
Save and load the stock data using C file handling (fopen, fprintf, fscanf), so the state survives between runs.
Add product prices and calculate the total cost of each order.
Add functions to register new products, dealers and retailers at runtime.
Keep a simple order history log so past transactions can be reviewed.
Add low-stock warnings when a product falls below a threshold.
8. Conclusion

The Distribution Management System achieves everything it set out to do. It models a realistic three-level supply chain, enforces sensible rules on every stock transfer, and presents its information in clean, readable console tables. More importantly, it proves that a well-structured, multi-file program does not require advanced language features: the entire system is built from arrays, loops, conditionals and functions. Working on this project gave practical experience in dividing a problem into modules, sharing data between source files with extern declarations, validating user input, and designing text output that people can actually read. The final program compiles cleanly with GCC and behaved correctly in all ten test scenarios.
